content.p: In April 2005 Indonesian police arrested nine Australians in Bali on suspicion of trying to move heroin out of the island and into Australia. Several of them were caught at Denpasar airport with packages strapped to their bodies, and others were picked up at a hotel in Kuta. The group became known in Australia as the "Bali Nine", a name the media gave it.

Two of the men, Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran, were sentenced to death by firing squad in February 2006. On 29 April 2015 they were shot on Nusa Kambangan, a prison island off Central Java, after their final appeals and clemency pleas had failed. Their executions caused a serious diplomatic dispute between Canberra and Jakarta. Nine years later, in December 2024, five of the men still held in Indonesia were flown home.

The Australian Federal Police had already passed information about the group to their Indonesian counterparts. SBS News reported that the AFP told them to "take whatever action you deem necessary". Lawyers for Lawrence and Rush later alleged that the AFP may have acted illegally by handing that information over, according to SBS.

The quantity of heroin was large. SBS and CNN put it at more than eight kilograms. NBC News, reporting the verdicts in 2006, gave the figure as more than 18 pounds. Indonesian police said Chan was the "godfather" of the operation, and two of the couriers said that he had threatened them with death if they refused to carry the drugs, SBS reported. Prosecutors called him the "driving engine" of the operation, according to NBC.

Police also shot and killed a Nepalese man, Mann Singh Gali, whom they said they believed had supplied the heroin. Prosecutors then confirmed that all nine Australians would be charged with possession and trafficking of heroin, offences that carried the death penalty.

The group was young, and most of its members came from Sydney and Brisbane. Chan was born in Sydney in 1984, the youngest child of parents who ran restaurants. He left school in year 10, worked for a catering company and later began smuggling drugs, according to Obituaries Australia. Sukumaran had dropped out of university. SBS reported that the chance of a "big pay cheque" came up while he was working in a Sydney mailroom.

Matthew Norman was the youngest of the group. Renae Lawrence, from Newcastle, was 28 at the time of the verdict, and the only woman among the nine. Martin Stephens, 29, came from Wollongong; Michael Czugaj, 20, came from Brisbane. Scott Rush, also from Brisbane, had been applying to enter the RAAF before he agreed to the trip, SBS reported. Tan Duc Thanh Nguyen's family ran a bakery in Brisbane, and SBS reported that he had recruited Rush and Czugaj on a night out there. Si Yi Chen, from Sydney, appears from SBS's account to have run errands for the ringleaders.
Obituaries Australia says that Chan told police he knew the other men but knew nothing about drugs. In court he said, "The truth is, I know nothing."

Each of the nine had a separate trial. On Monday 13 February 2006 the court jailed Lawrence for life, even though prosecutors had asked for 20 years because she had cooperated with investigators. Under Indonesian law it is not binding on judges, but NBC reported it is seen as a strong recommendation.

On the following day, Tuesday 14 February, the Denpasar District Court sentenced Chan and Sukumaran to death. Both verdicts matched what prosecutors had demanded. Sukumaran, prosecutors said, had helped strap the packages onto the couriers and had planned the operation. Chief judge Arif Supratman said of Chan: "There are no mitigating factors." He added that Chan's statements during the trial were convoluted and that he had not owned up to his actions.

The same week, Czugaj and Stephens received life sentences. Critic reported that the 2006 death sentences were the first time the Denpasar court had imposed the death penalty for drug trafficking. Australia's foreign minister, Alexander Downer, had asked Jakarta before the verdicts not to impose the death penalty on any of the group.

The sentences did not stay fixed. According to the SBS timeline, some of the men had their sentences cut to 20 years on appeal. Prosecutors then won their own appeal, and Rush, Nguyen, Chen and Norman were sentenced to death. Later, Nguyen, Chen and Norman had their death sentences reduced to life. The SBS timeline does not record a reduction for Rush, but by 2024 all five of the men later repatriated were serving life terms.

Chan's appeal was rejected by the Bali High Court in April 2006, Obituaries Australia reports. In August 2010 his lawyers asked for a judicial review of the death sentence, and that was also rejected. Obituaries Australia dates the Indonesian Supreme Court's rejection of his appeal against the sentence to June 2011.

The clemency process was slow and then closed. A petition with 150,000 signatures was handed to the families, and Australia's foreign minister, Julie Bishop, made an emotional plea in federal parliament, according to the SBS timeline. Joko Widodo, the new president, made clear that he would not grant clemency to drug traffickers. Chan and Sukumaran were moved from Bali's Kerobokan prison to Nusa Kambangan in March 2015.

Obituaries Australia reports that Chan converted to Christianity, ran drug counselling courses and conducted an English-language church service at Kerobokan. Sudjonggo, the Kerobokan governor, described them as model prisoners who should not be executed. In February 2015 Chan was ordained as a Christian minister in the prison chapel. Shortly after he was formally told of his execution, he married Febyanti Herewila in the Nusa Kambangan prison chapel.

Critic reports that the executions took place at 12:30 a.m. on Wednesday 29 April 2015, on Nusa Kambangan. SBS, citing Indonesian media, put the time at just after 3:30 a.m. Australian Eastern Standard Time. The two men were among eight people shot that day. SBS reported that Chan and Sukumaran were killed along with six other death row prisoners. Critic named six of the others: four Nigerians, a Brazilian, Rodrigo Gularte, and an Indonesian, Zainal Abidin. Mary Jane Veloso, the only woman in the group, was given a reprieve, and the Philippine Foreign Affairs Department confirmed she had been spared the firing squad for now.

According to Critic, there was a twelve-man firing squad, and the men chose not to wear blindfolds. They sang the chorus of "Amazing Grace" before they were shot. Critic reported that all eight men were confirmed dead at 1:02 a.m. Indonesian time.

Chan's brother Michael tweeted within minutes of the reports: "I have just lost a courageous brother to a flawed Indonesian legal system. I miss you already." Journalist Mark Davis, who had covered the case since 2010, told the ABC that the executions were a huge injustice. Phelim Kine, the deputy director of Human Rights Watch's Asia division, told the ABC he hoped Indonesia would go back to its unofficial moratorium on the death penalty.

Prime Minister Tony Abbott condemned the executions and withdrew Australia's ambassador from Indonesia for consultations, Critic reported. Foreign Minister Julie Bishop said she was "deeply disturbed" and that there "will have to be consequences". President Widodo, for his part, said the executions were needed to fight Indonesia's drug trafficking crisis.

Lawrence had 2.7 kilograms of heroin strapped to her body when she was arrested at Denpasar airport, CNN reported. She was first given a life sentence, but on appeal, with the support of prosecutors, it was reduced to 20 years, largely because she cooperated with investigators and identified the roles of other members of the group, Malay Mail reported from Reuters. CNN reported that she did not appeal the 20-year sentence. According to CNN, she has said Chan had threatened her life unless she joined the scheme.

Lawrence left Bangli prison on 21 November 2018, after 13 years, through a media scrum. Malay Mail reports that remissions cut a further seven years from her time in prison. Bali's Justice Office chief, Maryoto Sumadi, said she would not be allowed to return to Indonesia. She was also facing two outstanding warrants in New South Wales, reportedly relating to a high-speed chase in a stolen car before she left for Bali. A New South Wales police spokeswoman told Reuters that the warrants related to traffic offences.
Tan Duc Thanh Nguyen died of cancer in 2018, and CNN says it was in prison. SBS and Malay Mail also report the death: SBS gives no month, and Malay Mail says May.
content.h2: The return of five men in 2024
content.p: On Sunday 15 December 2024, Czugaj, Chen, Stephens, Rush and Norman were transferred from Bali and landed in Darwin. SBS reported that they had served more than 19 years in Indonesia's prison system. Indonesia's government said they were transferred with the status of prisoners.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described the move as made "on humanitarian grounds". He said the men "will now have the opportunity to continue their personal rehabilitation and reintegration here in Australia." Yusril Ihza Mahendra, Indonesia's senior minister for legal affairs, described the arrangement as reciprocal, and said the five men were barred for life from entering Indonesia.

The reports do not agree on every detail. The amount of heroin is given as more than eight kilograms by SBS and CNN, and as more than 18 pounds by NBC. SBS says the airport arrests included Chan, while CNN says Chan was taken after boarding a plane to Sydney, and NBC says he was arrested inside a Sydney-bound flight. SBS says Chan and Sukumaran were killed along with six other death row prisoners; Critic says there were eight other men, but the names it lists add up to six.
The month of Nguyen's death is also disputed. SBS gives 2018 without a month, Malay Mail places it in May and CNN in June.
